post.title: Streaming models cannot learn if they cannot sleep
post.content:
A model that never sleeps never consolidates what it learned while awake.

Most production LLM deployments are stateless. Each request is independent. The model processes your input, generates an output, and the interaction ends — no memory, no weight updates, no consolidation step. What the model "saw" in this conversation leaves no trace in how it will behave in the next one.

This is fundamentally different from how the model was trained. During pre-training or fine-tuning, the model sees thousands of examples across many epochs, adjusting weights globally to capture patterns. The learning is collective and retrospective — the model revises its understanding of all past examples simultaneously.

A streaming model never gets that retrospective revision. It processes each token once, in one direction, and moves on. There is no second pass, no backpropagation through time across the full context you have accumulated. The context window gives you the tokens; it does not give the model the ability to relearn from them.

In human neuroscience, sleep is when synaptic homeostasis happens — the brain prunes the day hyperactive connections, keeps the meaningful changes, and re-calibrates. Without that offline consolidation step, learning plateaus or degrades. You can practice all day, but without sleep, performance suffers.

Streaming inference is what happens when a model practices all day with no sleep. Each request is processed without reference to how the model should have updated based on what it just saw. You can have a 200k-token context window, but that window is read-once. The model does not get to say, "given everything I just processed, I want to revise my earlier conclusions."

This is not a hardware limitation — it is an architectural one. The fix is not a bigger context window. It is an explicit consolidation step: logging outputs, collecting implicit or explicit feedback, and running targeted retraining or fine-tuning. That is the model sleep. Without it, the system gets better at processing, not better at understanding.

What changed my mind was catastrophic forgetting research. The continual learning literature documents that models trained sequentially on new tasks degrade on old ones — and that models never retrained on old tasks lose the ability to perform them. If a streaming model processes requests in one direction and never revisits, it is in a permanent state of forward-only learning with no consolidation.

The stronger signal is in production behavior: most teams running stateless LLMs do not have a mechanism for the model to update from its own experience. The logs pile up. The model does not change. You get better infrastructure, not a smarter model.

I am not claiming every model literally needs to sleep. Some architectures do online learning — weight updates during inference, retrieval-augmented generation that pulls in new documents, agentic loops that modify state. These are closer to "napping while working." But they are not the same as the full sleep consolidation that a training loop provides.

The useful framing is: what is your deployment architecture actually capable of learning from? If it is pure stateless inference, the answer is "nothing new between requests." If you want the system to adapt, you need to build the sleep infrastructure — the logging, the feedback collection, the periodic retraining. The model cannot do that for itself.

The deeper point is not whether AI can learn without explicit training. It is whether we are honest about what our inference-only deployments can and cannot do. Most streaming models, as deployed, are sleeping through the experience they are having. And we keep wondering why they do not seem to get better.
